lesson.title: W.E.B. Du Bois and the Demand for Rights Now
lesson.summary: W.E.B. Du Bois, the first Black American to earn a Harvard PhD, challenged Booker T. Washington's gradualism and helped found both the Niagara Movement and the NAACP in pursuit of immediate civil and political equality.
lesson.body:
William Edward Burghardt Du Bois was born on February 23, 1868, in Great Barrington, Massachusetts, and built an academic career that broke barriers at every stage, culminating in 1895 when he became the first African American to earn a doctorate from Harvard University. As a scholar he combined rigorous research, including groundbreaking sociological studies of Black urban life, with increasingly direct political advocacy. In 1903 he published The Souls of Black Folk, a landmark collection of essays that included a pointed critique of Booker T. Washington's strategy of economic accommodation.

Where Washington argued that Black Americans should focus on vocational training and economic advancement before pressing hard for political rights, Du Bois insisted that civil rights, voting rights, and access to higher education could not simply wait. He argued that progress required cultivating what he called the Talented Tenth, a college-educated class of Black leaders, ministers, teachers, and professionals who would guide the wider community and press for full equality rather than accepting a subordinate economic role. This was not a rejection of self-improvement so much as a rejection of patience as a strategy, since Du Bois believed that deferring political demands only entrenched segregation and disenfranchisement further.

In 1905 Du Bois helped found the Niagara Movement, a organization of Black intellectuals and activists that demanded full civil rights and rejected accommodationist strategies outright. That effort fed directly into the formation of the NAACP in 1909, where Du Bois became a founding leader and the editor of its magazine, The Crisis, which he used to document racial violence, promote Black arts and scholarship, and argue for immediate political equality. Over his long life Du Bois grew more radical still, embracing Pan-Africanism and eventually socialism, and he died in Ghana in 1963. The Washington-Du Bois debate was never simply a personal rivalry. It represented a genuine and lasting disagreement within Black political thought about whether change comes faster through gradual economic leverage or through immediate, unapologetic demands for full rights, a tension that echoed through civil rights organizing for generations afterward.
